newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore February industrial output falls 5.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore February industrial output falls 5.5 pct.

text.p: Singapore's industrial output is still falling after a slowdown in the global electronics industry, figures published on Thursday showed.
The Economic Development Board (EDB) said manufacturing production fell 5.5 percent in February year-on-year, after dropping 6.9 percent in January.

The EDB said the drop, the fourth consecutive monthly fall, reflected a slowdown in the output of electronics, machinery, transport equipment, plastics, fabricated metal products, petroleum products and electrical machinery and appliances.
Singapore's key electronics industry continued to decline.
The Singapore economy is heavily dependent on electronics and related products, which account for around half its industrial output and about 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
"Some segments of the electronics industry remained depressed," the EDB said in a statement.
"Overall (electronics) output declined by 7.8 percent with decreased output from the semiconductors, consumer electronics and PCBA (printed circuit board assembly) segments."
Cumulative electronics output for the first two months of 1997 was 9.6 percent lower than in the same period in 1996.
Thursday's figures were close to market expectations.
Economists had predicted February's industrial output data would show a fall of between four and 12 percent on the year, with most estimates around minus seven or eight percent.

Prasenjit Basu, regional economist at Union Bank of Switzerland, said the figures looked bad but actually suggested the Singapore economy was recovering gradually from a slump which took hold in the third quarter of 1996.

"February probably marks the bottom of the economic cycle," Basu said. "We are beginning to see the start of a very modest pick up in demand in the electronics sector which should feed through to growth later in the year."
Singapore's electronics sector began to suffer in the middle of 1996 after a downturn in the dominant U.S. electronics industry, to which Singapore-based firms sell much of their production.
The U.S. industry began to recover in the third quarter of last year and economists expect this to filter down the supply chain to East Asia over the next few months.

Most economists still expect the Singapore economy to expand by four to 4.5 percent in the first quarter of this year, by 5.5 to six percent in the second quarter and by around seven percent in the second half of the year.
Singapore's annual growth is estimated by economists at between six and seven percent for 1997, slightly higher than the government's official forecast of five to seven percent.
The Singapore economy grew seven percent in 1996.
"I'm looking for a general economic recovery sometime in the second half," said Eddie Lee, economist at Singapore brokerage Vickers Ballas.
